articles.title: It's a 5% world. We're just living in it
articles.description: The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher , with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook. The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%. Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption. It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades. Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over. Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government. While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last. Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance. Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation. Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative. The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages. State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans. Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000. Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up. People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust. The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier. The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained. By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills. But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that. In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline. Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time. So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump). The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital. And that adjustment is in its early days.

articles.title: Trump faces legal reckoning as desperate plea for love breaks federal law
articles.description: Sabrina Haake is a political analyst and 25+ year federal trial attorney specializing in 1st and 14th A defense. Subscribe to her free Substack, The Haake Take . Thursday’s ruling from U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly putting an end to Trump’s White House media ban was lamentable for the speed with which it was issued. An exhausted nation was enjoying a break from Trump’s vitriol dominating every channel but, alas, the reprieve was short-lived. On September 24, only three days after banned outlets CNN, MSN, and Politico sued , Kelly ordered the White House to ‘immediately return, reinstate, and restore’ their access to the White House. The judge said the banned media outlets had met the legal thresholds for a temporary restraining order , which he put into effect for 14 days. “This is a high bar,” Kelly wrote, “but Plaintiffs have met it.” At argument, Trump’s DOJ made a laughable attempt to call his press ban a “matter of national security.” The DOJ argued that the three banned news organizations engaged in a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” that “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.” Those incidents included publishing construction details about the East Wing bunker, reporting on who is really funding the White House ballroom, and reports detailing how U.S. munitions stockpiles were affected by the administration’s mistakes in Iran. Kelly rejected the DOJ’s “national security” explanation as an after-the-fact justification. The judge noted that Trump had not used a national security argument when he announced the ban, but instead focused solely on what Trump called negative coverage of his administration. Trump TV: when a man gasps for attention like a fish out of water On the day of the hearing Wednesday , after Kelly had failed to immediately rule , even though the ban was a textbook example of government censorship, I was hopeful the judge would drag his decision out, because other major news networks had suspended their shared pooled television coverage of Trump in solidarity with the banned networks. The media boycott left Trump with comically reduced media exposure as even The New York Times and The Washington Post stopped publishing new Trump images . The media blackout was so effective, it seemed perhaps Kelly, a Trump appointee, might have a partisan motive in prolonging it: to help Republican candidates in competitive races by reducing Trump’s face time. A delayed ruling meant continued diminished Trump coverage, also a welcome balm for our collective mental health. But taking airtime from a creature formed by Reality TV and media attention was like taking a fish out of water. Deprived of 24/7 media attention, Trump’s pitiful wet flopping on the deck prompted his staff to create a quick and embarrassing replacement: Trump TV , a 24-hour YouTube livestream of White House coverage — curated, of course, by the White House. Trump calls himself the “King of Ratings,” but Trump TV debuted to hilariously small numbers, peaking at around 8,000 viewers and frequently dropping down to a few thousand. As of Thursday morning, under 500 live viewers were watching. The internet blew up over the fact that a YouTube stream of a black screen and box fan had more viewers than Trump. One of the funniest sentences ever written, thank you Roxanne Cooper of Alternet , said it all: “Trump TV was similarly crushed by random ambient streams of people getting pedicures.” And now, a blatantly illegal campaign ad Trump’s lesson in humility would be funny, but Trump has taken State TV to the next illegal level. Fox News is now airing a new partisan ad promoting Trump , “paid for by the U.S. government.” The 30-second video combines rapid cuts of Trump, American flags, and military aircraft, alongside claims about tax cuts, manufacturing, and policing. Images of Trump are accompanied by a choir singing, “Love me,” repeatedly. It ends with Dana White saying, “He is the toughest, most resilient person I’ve ever met, and nothing was going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country he loves.” Spending tax dollars on political campaign ads has long been illegal under federal law. The Hatch Act prohibits federal employees , as well as local government employees under federally funded programs, from engaging in political activities of any kind while they are on the clock. The General Government Appropriations Act also prohibits the expenditure of any tax dollars to produce partisan content. Ads that glorify an official or an administration, like singing “Love me” against a backdrop of militaristic Trump images and brags, blatantly violate both laws. Internet reaction was swift and correct. Occupy Democrats' Grant Stern tweeted , “Dear Leader is using YOUR tax dollars to make this insane propaganda with a musical track that says 'Love Me' on repeat.” Author Brendan Noble asked , “Why is the U.S. Government paying for cult-level media like this? 'Love me' over images of Trump feels like some weird psychological play. Regardless, it's propaganda with our tax dollars.” The cost of the absence of truth The ad is an obviously illegal use of taxpayer dollars, and a legal reckoning will come at some point, IF the 90 million voters who stayed home in 2024 care more about the price of gas than they cared about Trump’s J6 coup attempt. But more dangerous than Trump’s continued abuse of power is the fact that Trump appears to believe his own falsehoods. Much noise has been made about Trump’s assistant Natalie Harp , who follows him around with a portable printer. It’s widely reported that Harp shows Trump only favorable news stories, positive polling, and praise. Trump inhales that disinformation and regurgitates it back to a press pool allergic to hard questions because they are owned by Trump’s corporate backers. Steady flattery may make the job more palatable to a man getting tired of politics, but it’s dangerous. Trump can’t make informed decisions if he only hears information he wants to hear; advisors with nefarious intentions can also shape information to manipulate him. But that’s what seems to be happening: Trump believes we are winning the war in Iran because Hegseth tells him we are; he believes the economy is strong ; he thinks world leaders respect him, even as they mock him and move toward alliances excluding the U.S. Unfavored media outlets’ crucial role is correcting Trump’s misinformation on everything — the war in Iran , the economy , even foreign trade . They may have returned to the White House, but the extreme danger of a president so insulated from the truth that he believes his own propaganda remains.

articles.title: Todd Blanche admitted breaking Epstein files law in his own court filing: Katie Phang
articles.description: Attorney General Todd Blanche admitted in a court filing that he violated the Epstein files law, according to the journalist suing him. Journalist and lawyer Katie Phang made the claim in a Saturday video posted on her YouTube channel, "Katie Phang News," as she walked viewers through Blanche's answer to her lawsuit seeking the unredacted Epstein files. The key passage, she said, came in Blanche's response to her complaint, which alleged the Justice Department pulled previously released documents relating to President Donald Trump. Blanche admitted that "at times specific discrete documents were removed from the Epstein library," citing material posted "without redaction where redaction was appropriate whether by a victim or a member of the public." Phang argued nothing in the law allows that. "Where in the Epstein Files Transparency Act did it say that Todd Blanche could redact or withhold because it revealed the name of a member of the public?" she asked. "There is now an admission in a federal case that Todd Blanche has violated the Epstein Files Transparency Act," Phang said. "Again, I mean, not like we needed any more proof, but there's his own admission that he's violated the law." Phang also mocked Blanche's description of Trump in the filing as "the leader of the most transparent presidential administration in the history of this great nation." "Even when Todd Blanche is being sued, he can't take off his a— kisser hat, can he?" she said. She said Blanche's answer to her complaint turned personal. In one section, Blanche called an allegation from the files, that a woman accused Trump of abusing her as a minor, "sensationalized and spurious." He said it appeared "only to be a vehicle" for Phang and her attorneys "to attack their political opponents." Trump has long denied wrongdoing in connection with Epstein. Blanche also argued in an affirmative defense that Phang's "ability to do her job has been unchanged," noting she "has even appeared on cable TV to discuss this case." Phang said that misstates her claim. "I am not restrained from speaking about this topic, but I am most certainly prevented from being able to do my job to investigate further," she said. She added that the tone of the filing only encouraged her. "Frankly, I'm tickled pink that these people have now made it so personal that they want to attack me in their answer," Phang said. "Now that he has answered, we are more than one step closer to a final resolution of this lawsuit."
